items.stem: ‘Stalin was mainly responsible for the Cold War.’ How far do you agree with this view?

items.stem: The following extract is from a historian writing in the 1950s (illustrative). “Within months of Yalta, the Soviet Union had broken its promise of free elections in Poland and was installing obedient communist governments across Eastern Europe. Stalin's ideology taught him that conflict with the capitalist world was inevitable, and he expanded wherever he met no resistance. The Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan were the West's belated response.” What can you learn from this extract about the interpretation and approach of the historian who wrote it? Use the extract and your knowledge of the origins of the Cold War to explain your answer.
items.answer: Interpretation: Soviet expansionism, driven by Stalin and communist ideology, caused the Cold War, and the USA responded defensively. Approach: The historian focuses on Soviet ideology and actions in Eastern Europe, judging the USSR by its breaches of wartime agreements. Own knowledge that supports it: Yalta promised free elections, which were not held in Poland. Communist takeovers, as in Czechoslovakia in 1948. The Berlin Blockade of 1948-49. Own knowledge that challenges it: The USSR lost about 27 million people and sought security. The 1944 percentages agreement accepted Soviet influence in Romania and Bulgaria. Stalin gave little help to Greek communists and withdrew from Iran in 1946. Context: Orthodox accounts were written in the USA in the late 1940s and 1950s, during the early Cold War and McCarthyism, often by historians close to government.

items.stem: What is meant by “Open Door”?
options: The use of the US monopoly of the atomic bomb to put pressure on the USSR.
Misunderstanding of the motives and actions of another state.
The organisation set up by Stalin in 1947 to coordinate communist parties.
The US aim of an open world economy in which American goods and capital could move freely.
items.answer: The US aim of an open world economy in which American goods and capital could move freely.
items.markingKey: Open Door: the US aim of an open world economy in which American goods and capital could move freely. [1]

items.stem: Explain one reason why revisionist historians blamed the USA for the Cold War.
items.answer: US leaders sought an open world economy that threatened Soviet control.
items.markingKey: For each reason: 1 mark for identifying it and 1 mark for explaining it with supporting detail, from: US leaders sought an open world economy that threatened Soviet control. The atomic bomb was used partly to intimidate the USSR. The Truman Doctrine exaggerated the Soviet threat to win support in Congress. The Marshall Plan divided Europe economically. The Vietnam War encouraged scepticism of US motives. [2]

items.stem: Elena is planning an answer to the question: “How far was the Marshall Plan an act of economic imperialism?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Elena could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: it served US economic and political interests, but it was also a genuine recovery programme that Europeans welcomed. Support: It opened European markets to US goods. It tied recipients to US economic policy. Challenge: It was offered to all of Europe, including the USSR. It helped European recovery and was welcomed.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: The following extract is from a historian writing in the late 1950s (illustrative). “American leaders believed that the prosperity of the United States depended on an open world economy. The Open Door, not the Iron Curtain, was the starting point of their policy. The Marshall Plan offered aid on terms that would tie Europe to American markets, and Moscow could hardly be expected to accept them.” How far does your own knowledge support the interpretation in the extract? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Supporting evidence: The USA sought free trade through Bretton Woods. Marshall Aid required economic openness. Soviet rejection of the plan followed from its terms. Challenging evidence: Soviet control of Eastern Europe preceded the Marshall Plan. The Plan was offered to the USSR. Stalin's ideology was hostile regardless of US economics. Judgement: the interpretation is supported in part; its strength depends on the evidence it emphasises.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the interpretation; up to 3 marks for own knowledge that supports it and up to 3 for knowledge that challenges it, each linked to the extract; 1 mark for a supported judgement [8]

items.stem: Study the extract. “American leaders believed that the prosperity of the United States depended on an open world economy. What can you learn from this extract about the interpretation and approach of the historian who wrote it? Use the extract and your knowledge of the origins of the Cold War to explain your answer.
items.answer: Interpretation: US economic expansion and the pursuit of an open world economy caused the Cold War. Approach: The historian focuses on US economic interests and policy, treating Soviet actions as responses. Own knowledge that supports it: The USA sought free trade through Bretton Woods. Marshall Aid required economic openness. Soviet rejection of the plan followed from its terms. Own knowledge that challenges it: Soviet control of Eastern Europe preceded the Marshall Plan. The Plan was offered to the USSR. Stalin's ideology was hostile regardless of US economics. Context: Revisionism developed in the USA from the late 1950s, influenced by W. A. Williams, and grew during the Vietnam War, when many questioned US foreign policy.

items.stem: In a revision class, a student says: “Soviet archives were fully open to historians in the 1950s.” Is this accurate? Explain your answer using your own knowledge.
items.answer: Not accurate. They became partly accessible only after 1991.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a correct judgement; 1 mark for accurate supporting knowledge [2]

items.stem: Which of these events happened last?
options: The USSR tested its first atomic bomb
items.answer: The USSR tested its first atomic bomb
items.markingKey: The USSR tested its first atomic bomb (August 1949); the Truman Doctrine was announced (12 March 1947); the Berlin Blockade began (24 June 1948); NATO was founded (April 1949). [1]

items.stem: Samuel is planning an answer to the question: “How far has the opening of Soviet archives changed interpretations of the origins of the Cold War?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Samuel could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: the archives shifted the balance towards Stalin's responsibility, but they did not end the debate. Support: It revealed Stalin's ideological outlook and suspicion. It showed Soviet direction of Eastern European communists. Challenge: Much remains closed or fragmentary. It confirmed Soviet security fears stressed by revisionists.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: Study the extract. “Neither side sought a Cold War. Each acted to secure itself, and each read the other's defensive moves as offensive. American leaders, constrained by Congress and public opinion, oversold the Soviet threat; Stalin's search for a security belt in Eastern Europe looked like expansion from Washington.” (A historian writing in 1972 (illustrative).) Use your knowledge of the origins of the Cold War to explain how far the evidence supports the interpretation in the extract.
items.answer: Supporting evidence: Soviet security concerns after invasion in 1941. US domestic politics shaped rhetoric such as the Truman Doctrine. Each side misread the other's actions. Challenging evidence: Soviet archives later showed ideological hostility. Soviet takeovers went beyond security needs. Some US actions were driven by economic interest. Judgement: the interpretation is supported in part; its strength depends on the evidence it emphasises.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the interpretation; up to 3 marks for own knowledge that supports it and up to 3 for knowledge that challenges it, each linked to the extract; 1 mark for a supported judgement [8]

items.stem: In 1972 John Lewis Gaddis published The United States and the Origins of the Cold War, 1941-1947. How far has the opening of Soviet archives changed interpretations of the origins of the Cold War?
items.answer: For: It revealed Stalin's ideological outlook and suspicion. It showed Soviet direction of Eastern European communists. It led Gaddis and others to put more weight on Stalin. Against: Much remains closed or fragmentary. It confirmed Soviet security fears stressed by revisionists. US evidence and economic factors remain important. Judgement: the archives shifted the balance towards Stalin's responsibility, but they did not end the debate.

items.stem: A revision website states: “Orthodox accounts were written with full access to Soviet archives.” Is this accurate? Explain your answer using your own knowledge.

items.markingKey: 1 mark for a correct judgement; 1 mark for accurate supporting knowledge [2]

items.stem: Read the extract and then answer the question. Extract: a historian writing in the 1960s (illustrative). “In February 1946 Stalin told Soviet voters that war was inevitable while capitalism survived. Two weeks later Kennan explained to Washington that Soviet power was impervious to reason but sensitive to force. American policy thereafter was a response to a threat that Moscow had chosen to make.” What is the main interpretation of the historian in the extract? Support your answer with two details from the extract.
items.answer: Interpretation: The Cold War was a response to a Soviet threat deliberately created by Stalin's hostility to the West. Support from the extract: for example, “In February 1946 Stalin told Soviet voters that war was inevitable while capitalism survived.”
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a sub-message; 2 marks for the main interpretation; up to 2 marks for supporting detail from the extract [4]

items.stem: Daniel is planning an answer to the question: “How far was the Cold War caused by the Soviet takeover of Eastern Europe?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Daniel could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: the takeover of Eastern Europe was the central issue that turned wartime tension into Cold War. Support: It broke the Declaration on Liberated Europe. It created the Iron Curtain. Challenge: The Western allies had accepted Soviet influence in the percentages agreement. Disputes over Germany and reparations mattered as much.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.answer: Interpretation: The Cold War was a response to a Soviet threat deliberately created by Stalin's hostility to the West. Approach: The historian uses statements by Soviet and American leaders to show that the USA reacted to Soviet hostility. Own knowledge that supports it: Stalin's election speech of February 1946. Kennan's Long Telegram. Soviet pressure on Turkey and Iran in 1946. Own knowledge that challenges it: Speeches were for domestic audiences. US policy also had economic motives. Western statements, such as Churchill's Iron Curtain speech, also raised tension.

Misunderstanding of the motives and actions of another state.

items.stem: In a revision class, a student says: “The first US atomic test took place the day before the Potsdam Conference opened.” Is this accurate? Explain your answer using your own knowledge.
items.answer: Accurate. The Trinity test was on 16 July 1945; Potsdam opened on 17 July. Revisionists argue Truman timed the conference with this in mind.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a correct judgement; 1 mark for accurate supporting knowledge [2]

items.stem: Historians have offered several reasons why revisionist historians blamed the USA for the Cold War. A: The Truman Doctrine exaggerated the Soviet threat to win support in Congress. B: The Vietnam War encouraged scepticism of US motives. C: The atomic bomb was used partly to intimidate the USSR. Explain how these reasons were linked and decide which mattered most.
items.answer: Any reasoned choice. A: The Truman Doctrine exaggerated the Soviet threat to win support in Congress. B: The Vietnam War encouraged scepticism of US motives. C: The atomic bomb was used partly to intimidate the USSR. Possible judgement: they saw US economic expansion as the driving force, a view encouraged by the context of the Vietnam War.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a choice; up to 3 marks for explaining it with precise detail; up to 2 marks for comparing it with the other reasons [6]

items.stem: The following extract is from a historian writing in 1965 (illustrative). “The bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki were aimed as much at Moscow as at Tokyo. The President delayed the meeting at Potsdam until the atomic test had succeeded, and his advisers believed the bomb would make the Russians more manageable in Europe. Atomic diplomacy convinced Stalin that the West meant to deny him security.” What can you learn from this extract about the interpretation and approach of the historian who wrote it? Use the extract and your knowledge of the origins of the Cold War to explain your answer.
items.answer: Interpretation: The USA used atomic diplomacy to pressure the USSR, which convinced Stalin of Western hostility. Approach: The historian focuses on US policy and decision-making, especially the use of the atomic bomb. Own knowledge that supports it: Potsdam began the day after the Trinity test. Byrnes believed the bomb would strengthen the US hand. The US monopoly lasted until 1949. Own knowledge that challenges it: The bomb was used mainly to end the war quickly and save US lives. Soviet actions in Poland came before the bomb. Stalin already knew of the project through spies.

items.stem: A revision website states: “Gaddis's later work put more weight on Stalin's responsibility.” Is this accurate? Explain your answer using your own knowledge.
items.answer: Accurate. We Now Know (1997) argued that Stalin's personality and ideology made the Cold War likely.

items.stem: Study the extract. “Neither side sought a Cold War. Each acted to secure itself, and each read the other's defensive moves as offensive. American leaders, constrained by Congress and public opinion, oversold the Soviet threat; Stalin's search for a security belt in Eastern Europe looked like expansion from Washington.” (A historian writing in 1972 (illustrative).) Which of these best describes the approach of the historian who wrote the extract?
options: Focus on mutual perceptions and security fears
Use of newly opened Soviet archives
Focus on US economic interests and policy
Focus on Soviet ideology and actions in Eastern Europe
items.answer: Focus on mutual perceptions and security fears
items.markingKey: The historian focuses on mutual perceptions and security fears, using US government records. [1]

items.stem: A revision guide lists these reasons why post-revisionist interpretations emerged in the 1970s. A: Research showed both sides acted from security fears. B: Historians sought a middle ground after the polarised orthodox-revisionist debate. C: Newly released US government records gave a fuller picture of decision-making. Which was the most significant? Explain your answer with reference to the other reasons.
items.answer: Any reasoned choice. A: Research showed both sides acted from security fears. B: Historians sought a middle ground after the polarised orthodox-revisionist debate. C: Newly released US government records gave a fuller picture of decision-making. Possible judgement: new US evidence and the less tense climate of détente encouraged a more balanced view.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a choice; up to 3 marks for explaining it with precise detail; up to 2 marks for comparing it with the other reasons [6]

items.stem: The following extract is from a historian writing in 1997 (illustrative). “The opening of the Soviet archives has changed the debate. They show a Stalin who saw the world through the lens of Marxist-Leninist ideology, who distrusted even his allies, and who probed for advantage wherever he could. As long as Stalin ruled, a Cold War was probably unavoidable.” How far does your own knowledge support the interpretation in the extract? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Supporting evidence: Archives show Stalin's suspicion of the West. Soviet direction of Eastern European communist parties. Stalin approved the Berlin Blockade and later the Korean War. Challenging evidence: The archives also show Soviet security fears. Some archives remain closed. US policy also contributed. Judgement: the interpretation is supported in part; its strength depends on the evidence it emphasises.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the interpretation; up to 3 marks for own knowledge that supports it and up to 3 for knowledge that challenges it, each linked to the extract; 1 mark for a supported judgement [8]

items.answer: Interpretation: Both superpowers contributed to the Cold War through mutual misperception and the pursuit of security. Approach: The historian focuses on mutual perceptions and security fears, using US government records. Own knowledge that supports it: Soviet security concerns after invasion in 1941. Soviet takeovers went beyond security needs. Some US actions were driven by economic interest. Context: Post-revisionism emerged in the 1970s, drawing on newly released US records and seeking a middle ground after the Vietnam-era debate.
